blurb: Milestone moments from Magna Carta to the modern era

questions.q: In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west for the rulers of which country?
questions.fact: His three ships were the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria.
questions.src: Textbook (voyage backed by Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile and Aragon, i.e. Spain); reworded from 'flag of which kingdom'

questions.q: Which Portuguese explorer became the first European to reach India by sea, in 1498?
questions.fact: He reached Calicut after rounding Africa's Cape of Good Hope, first passed by Dias in 1488.
questions.src: Textbook (da Gama reached Calicut May 1498; Dias rounded the Cape 1488). Writer's Wikipedia for Schools note agrees

questions.q: Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 Kon-Tiki expedition crossed the Pacific from Peru on what kind of vessel?
questions.fact: The raft traveled about 4,300 miles in 101 days before reaching an atoll in French Polynesia.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kon-Tiki_expedition: nine balsa logs, Callao to Raroia (Tuamotus, French Polynesia), 101 days, ~4,300 mi

questions.q: A 2021 tree-ring study showed Vikings were cutting wood in Newfoundland in which year?
questions.fact: Scientists counted rings from a radiation spike caused by a solar storm in 993 to pin the exact year.
questions.src: nationalgeographic.com ancient-solar-storm-pinpoints-viking-settlement: trees felled AD 1021, dated by counting rings from the 993 solar-storm spike

questions.q: Who was the main author of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.fact: Most delegates actually signed it on August 2, 1776, not July 4.
questions.src: nps.gov/articles/engrossed.htm: most members signed the engrossed copy Aug 2, 1776; Jefferson as main drafter is textbook

questions.q: In 1215, English barons forced which king to agree to Magna Carta?
questions.fact: Four original 1215 copies survive: two at the British Library and one each at Lincoln and Salisbury.
questions.src: medieval.eu/magna-cartas-united: four 1215 copies survive, two at the British Library, one each at Lincoln and Salisbury cathedrals

questions.q: Which Founding Father wrote 51 of the 85 Federalist Papers?
questions.fact: Madison wrote 29 and John Jay wrote five, all under the shared pen name Publius.
questions.src: battlefields.org Federalist Papers: Hamilton 51, Madison 29, Jay 5, pen name Publius

questions.q: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands between Spain and which country?
questions.fact: Its line gave Portugal a claim to eastern South America, one reason Brazil speaks Portuguese.
questions.src: Textbook (Tordesillas 1494, Castile and Portugal; line put eastern Brazil on Portugal's side)

questions.q: Declared complete in 2003, the Human Genome Project mapped the full set of human what?
questions.fact: It finished in April 2003, 50 years after Watson and Crick described DNA's double helix.
questions.src: genome.gov 2003 release: HGP declared complete April 14, 2003; Watson-Crick paper was April 1953 (moved from $300 to $100)

questions.q: In 2012, scientists at CERN announced the discovery of which long-sought particle?
questions.fact: Peter Higgs, one of the physicists who predicted it in 1964, shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics.
questions.src: pbs.org/wgbh/nova higgs-and-englert-win-physics-nobel-prize: CERN announcement July 4, 2012; Englert and Higgs shared 2013 Nobel; theory 1964. Neutron 1932, positron 1932, neutrino 1956

questions.q: Opened in 2000, the Oresund Bridge links Denmark with which country?
questions.fact: It ends on an artificial island, Peberholm, where the route continues through an undersea tunnel to Copenhagen.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oresund_Bridge: opened 1 July 2000, links Copenhagen and Malmo; bridge joins the Oresund Tunnel on Peberholm

questions.q: In 2022, explorers found the ship Endurance deep off Antarctica. Whose expedition ship was it?
questions.fact: It sank in 1915, yet all 28 crew were rescued. The wreck was found about 10,000 feet down.
questions.src: aljazeera.com 2022/3/9 Shackleton's lost ship: found at 3,008 m (9,869 ft), sank 1915, all 28 men survived

blurb: Inventions and the minds behind them, ancient to modern

questions.q: A candy bar melting in Percy Spencer's pocket near radar gear led to which invention?
questions.fact: Early commercial microwaves stood nearly six feet tall and weighed about 750 pounds.
questions.src: aps.org/apsnews/2015/10/first-patent-for-microwave: candy bar melted; Radarange nearly six feet tall, more than 750 lb

questions.q: Mold growing on a dish Alexander Fleming left out in 1928 led to which discovery?
questions.fact: Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, who made it a usable drug.
questions.src: Textbook (Fleming 1928; 1945 Nobel in Physiology or Medicine shared with Florey and Chain)

questions.q: Burrs stuck to his dog's fur inspired Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral to invent what?
questions.fact: The name blends two French words: velours, meaning velvet, and crochet, meaning hook.
questions.src: swissinfo.ch how-a-swiss-invention-hooked-the-world: 1941 walk, burrs on dog's fur, electrical engineer, velours + crochet

questions.q: In 1938, DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett accidentally discovered which slippery material?
questions.fact: He was working on refrigerants when the gas inside a cylinder turned into a white solid.
questions.src: lemelson.mit.edu/resources/roy-plunkett: assigned to new Freon refrigerants; April 6, 1938 TFE gas in a cylinder solidified into PTFE

questions.q: Which German inventor brought movable-type printing to Europe around 1440?
questions.fact: Movable type had already been used in China and Korea centuries before Gutenberg's press.
questions.src: Textbook (Gutenberg c. 1440; Bi Sheng movable type c. 1040, Korean metal type by 1377)

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin invented which device to protect buildings during storms?
questions.fact: Franklin never patented his inventions, preferring to share them freely.
questions.src: fi.edu Benjamin Franklin inventions: never patented any, believing they should be shared freely; pointed lightning rod

questions.q: Galileo didn't invent the telescope. A patent for one was first sought in 1608 in which country?
questions.fact: Galileo built his own in 1609 and soon discovered four of Jupiter's moons.
questions.src: aas.org 2017/10 invention of the telescope: Lippershey's patent application, 2 Oct 1608, States General of the Netherlands; Galileo built his own in 1609

questions.q: The Archimedes screw, named for the ancient Greek scientist, was mainly used to do what?
questions.fact: A screw turning inside a tube carries water upward a little with every rotation.
questions.src: Textbook (water-raising screw). Reworded: its origin is disputed (possible earlier Assyrian use), so q no longer says it came from Greece

questions.q: Inventor James Dyson is best known for reinventing which household appliance?
questions.fact: He built 5,127 prototypes before landing on his bagless cyclone design.
questions.src: dyson.com relentless engineering: 'Creating 5,127 prototypes, to reach the first bagless vacuum'

questions.q: Which company launched the Roomba robot vacuum in 2002?
questions.fact: iRobot was founded in 1990 by three robotics experts from MIT.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRobot: founded 1990 by Brooks, Angle and Greiner after MIT's AI Lab; Roomba unveiled Sept 2002

questions.q: The QR code was invented in Japan in 1994 to keep track of what?
questions.fact: Inventor Masahiro Hara got the idea during a lunchtime game of Go, with its black and white stones.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_code (1994, Denso Wave, to track automobile parts); wiki/Masahiro_Hara (idea came during a lunchtime game of go). Old fact 'QR = Quick Response' duplicated A8 monday-mixer-3

questions.q: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honored the invention of what?
questions.fact: Lithium-ion batteries first went on sale in 1991. Co-winner John Goodenough was 97 when he won.
questions.src: nobelprize.org 2019 chemistry press release (for lithium-ion batteries; first entered the market 1991); wiki/John_B._Goodenough (97 at award). Blue LED was Physics 2014

blurb: Pharaohs, philosophers, emperors and empire builders

questions.q: Which river was the lifeline of ancient Egypt?
questions.fact: Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'black land,' after the dark, rich soil left by the floods.
questions.src: Textbook Egyptology (Kemet = black land, from Nile silt)

questions.q: The Rosetta Stone helped scholars finally read which ancient writing?
questions.fact: It repeats one decree in three scripts. Jean-Francois Champollion cracked it in 1822.
questions.src: Textbook (hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek texts; Champollion 1822)

questions.q: In 1922, Howard Carter found whose nearly intact tomb in Egypt's Valley of the Kings?
questions.fact: The 1970s 'Treasures of Tutankhamun' tour drew huge crowds to American museums.
questions.src: Textbook (Carter, Nov 1922); neh.gov King Tut Comes to America: US tour Nov 1976-Apr 1979, 6+ million visitors

questions.q: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for which pharaoh?
questions.fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of this pyramid.
questions.src: Textbook (Khufu, c. 2560 BC). Math: 2560 BC to 30 BC ~2,530 yrs; 30 BC to 1969 ~2,000 yrs

questions.q: In Greek mythology, which god ruled the sea?
questions.fact: The Romans called him Neptune, the name later given to the eighth planet.
questions.src: Textbook mythology

questions.q: Legend says Rome was founded by Romulus and his twin brother. What was the twin's name?
questions.fact: In the story, a she-wolf nursed the twins. Tradition dates Rome's founding to 753 BC.
questions.src: Textbook Roman legend

questions.q: Which Greek philosopher tutored a teenage Alexander the Great?
questions.fact: Aristotle had studied under Plato, who in turn had been a student of Socrates.
questions.src: Textbook

questions.q: Hadrian's Wall, the Roman frontier begun in AD 122, stands in which modern country?
questions.fact: It ran about 73 miles coast to coast. A later Roman barrier, the Antonine Wall, crossed Scotland.
questions.src: english-heritage.org.uk faqs-hadrians-wall: begun AD 122, 73 miles, in northern England; Antonine Wall in what is now Scotland

questions.q: Mexico City stands on the site of which civilization's great capital?
questions.fact: Their capital, Tenochtitlan, was first built on small islands in Lake Texcoco.
questions.src: britannica.com/place/Tenochtitlan: Aztec capital at the site of modern Mexico City, originally on two small islands in Lake Texcoco. Replaces Machu Picchu Q (A4 around-the-world names 'The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu')

questions.q: China's first emperor was buried with an army of life-size soldiers made of what?
questions.fact: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an found the first of the figures in 1974.
questions.src: britannica.com/topic/terra-cotta-army: found March 1974 by farmers digging a well; life-size figures

questions.q: Cuneiform, one of the world's earliest writing systems, began in which region?
questions.fact: Scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay. Cuneiform means 'wedge-shaped.'
questions.src: Textbook (cuneiform from Latin cuneus, wedge; Sumer/Mesopotamia)

questions.q: The ancient Maya counting system was based on groups of which number?
questions.fact: The Maya also had a symbol for zero, often drawn as a shell.
questions.src: mayan.org/symbols/numbers: vigesimal (base-20) system; stylized shell = 0. Base 60 = Babylonian

blurb: For Veterans Day: the stories behind famous monuments and memorials

questions.q: The WWI armistice took effect on November 11, 1918, at what time of day?
questions.fact: It was the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month, which is why Veterans Day is November 11.
questions.src: prologue.blogs.archives.gov From Armistice to Veterans Day: 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month, 1918

questions.q: Before 1954, the US holiday on November 11 was known as what?
questions.fact: It was renamed Veterans Day in 1954 to honor American veterans of all wars.
questions.src: prologue.blogs.archives.gov From Armistice to Veterans Day: renamed June 1, 1954 to honor veterans of all wars

questions.q: Which flower became a worldwide symbol of remembrance for WWI veterans?
questions.fact: The tradition grew from 'In Flanders Fields,' a 1915 poem by Canadian doctor John McCrae.
questions.src: Textbook (remembrance poppy; McCrae's In Flanders Fields, May 1915); militarytimes.com history of a symbol

questions.q: Sentinels at Arlington's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier take how many steps before turning?
questions.fact: The 21 steps echo the 21-gun salute, the highest military honor that can be given.
questions.src: arlingtoncemetery.mil Changing of the Guard: exactly 21 steps, 21-second pauses; 21 symbolizes the highest military honor, the 21-gun salute. Added 'Arlington's' since the deck also has France's tomb

questions.q: Mount Rushmore, with the carved faces of four presidents, is in which state?
questions.fact: Each of the four faces is about 60 feet tall.
questions.src: bensguide.gpo.gov Mount Rushmore: 'The faces of the Presidents are 60 feet high'

questions.q: The 630-foot Gateway Arch, completed in 1965, stands in which city?
questions.fact: It honors westward expansion and is exactly as wide at its base as it is tall.
questions.src: nps.gov/jeff 50th year of completion (630 ft, completed Oct 28, 1965, westward expansion); wiki/Gateway_Arch (width and height both 630 ft)

questions.q: Which French engineer designed the iron framework inside the Statue of Liberty?
questions.fact: Sculptor Frederic Auguste Bartholdi designed the statue, which was dedicated in 1886.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty: Eiffel (with Koechlin) designed the iron truss frame; Bartholdi sculptor; dedicated Oct 28, 1886

questions.q: The National WWII Memorial, dedicated in 2004, has 56 granite pillars. What do they stand for?
questions.fact: It sits on the National Mall between the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument.
questions.src: nps.gov/places/national-world-war-ii-memorial: 56 pillars for the states, D.C. and territories; dedicated May 29, 2004; framed by Washington Monument and Lincoln Memorial

questions.q: Stonehenge, the ring of giant prehistoric stones, stands in which country?
questions.fact: Its smaller bluestones were hauled from Wales, about 150 miles away.
questions.src: smithsonianmag.com stonehenge-was-moved-wales: Preseli bluestones roughly 150 miles away

questions.q: In London, the name Big Ben officially belongs to what?
questions.fact: The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 for Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.
questions.src: parliament.uk Big Ben factsheet ('Big Ben is in fact the Great Bell'); kvia.com Big Ben fast facts (renamed Elizabeth Tower Sept 12, 2012 for the Diamond Jubilee)

questions.q: France's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier lies beneath which Paris monument?
questions.fact: A memorial flame there has been rekindled every evening since 1923.
questions.src: cheminsdememoire.gouv.fr/en/arc-de-triomphe: Unknown Soldier buried 1921; flame first lit Nov 11, 1923, revived every evening, never stopped even 1940-44

questions.q: The nightly Last Post ceremony, begun in 1928, takes place at which memorial in Ypres, Belgium?
questions.fact: The Menin Gate memorial was unveiled in 1927, the year before the ceremony began.
questions.src: lastpost.be/about (Menin Gate inaugurated 24 July 1927; Last Post Association's first ceremony 2 July 1928); eu.mission.gov.au lastpost. Vimy/Thiepval in France, Cenotaph in London

blurb: Washington State: symbols, scenery, history and homegrown legends

questions.q: Invented on Bainbridge Island in 1965, which game became Washington's official state sport in 2022?
questions.fact: It started on a backyard badminton court with ping-pong paddles and a plastic ball full of holes.
questions.src: usapickleball.org history (Bainbridge 1965, badminton court, table tennis paddles, perforated plastic ball); wiki List_of_Washington_state_symbols (state sport 2022)

questions.q: Washington's official state marine mammal, adopted in 2005, is which animal?
questions.fact: Second graders at Crescent Harbor Elementary in Oak Harbor spent two years pushing for it.
questions.src: leg.wa.gov state symbols, marine mammal: orca, 2005, two years of work by Crescent Harbor Elementary second graders, Oak Harbor

questions.q: In 1928 schoolchildren chose the meadowlark, but which bird became Washington's state bird in 1951?
questions.fact: Seven other states had also picked the meadowlark. In a later student vote, the goldfinch won.
questions.src: leg.wa.gov state symbols, bird: 1928 children chose meadowlark, seven other states had it; 1931 club vote picked goldfinch; 1951 children voted goldfinch, Legislature adopted

questions.q: What is Washington's official state gem?
questions.fact: Ginkgo Petrified Forest State Park near Vantage preserves ancient logs that turned to stone.
questions.src: leg.wa.gov state symbols, gem: petrified wood adopted 1975; historylink.org File 7396 (Ginkgo park one mile north of Vantage, petrified logs)

questions.q: What is the highest mountain in Washington?
questions.fact: Mount Rainier National Park, created in 1899, was the nation's fifth national park.
questions.src: nps.gov/mora America's Fifth Park: established March 2, 1899, 'the fifth oldest national park'; Rainier highest in WA is textbook

questions.q: Grand Coulee Dam was built across which river?
questions.fact: Woody Guthrie's 1941 song 'Roll On, Columbia, Roll On' became the state folk song in 1987.
questions.src: Textbook (Grand Coulee on the Columbia); wiki Roll_On,_Columbia,_Roll_On (written 1941 for BPA, state folk song 1987)

questions.q: Spokane's Expo '74 was the first world's fair built around which theme?
questions.fact: Spokane was the smallest city yet to host one, and the fairgrounds became Riverfront Park.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_'74: first environmentally themed world's fair; smallest host city at the time (until Knoxville 1982); site became Riverfront Park

questions.q: Which Washington community can be reached by land only by driving through Canada?
questions.fact: It sits on the tip of a peninsula that dips just south of the 49th parallel, the border line.
questions.src: en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Point_Roberts: only road in or out is through Canada; Tsawwassen Peninsula just below the 49th parallel

questions.q: Which aerospace giant was founded in Seattle in 1916?
questions.fact: William Boeing first called it Pacific Aero Products Co., renaming it the next year.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Boeing: incorporated as Pacific Aero Products Co. July 15, 1916; renamed Boeing Airplane Company April 1917

questions.q: Which holiday grew out of a celebration held in Spokane on June 19, 1910?
questions.fact: Sonora Smart Dodd created it to honor her father, a Civil War veteran who raised six children.
questions.src: historylink.org File 9458 and wiki Sonora_Smart_Dodd (June 19, 1910 Spokane; Civil War veteran father raised six children). Reworded: a 1908 Fairmont, W.Va. service is also called the first Father's Day

questions.q: Which famous crooner grew up in Spokane and attended Gonzaga?
questions.fact: His boyhood home, built in 1911, became a museum on Gonzaga's campus.
questions.src: gonzaga.edu Bing Crosby House Museum: home built 1911, now a Gonzaga museum; Bing entered Gonzaga in fall 1920

questions.q: Amazon was founded in 1994 in a garage in which Washington city?
questions.fact: Amazon says its first desks there were made from wooden doors with legs attached.
questions.src: historylink.org File 23230 (rented Bellevue house, garage, 1994); aboutamazon.com first-amazon-office (door desks). Old 'only books' fact duplicated A2 log-on Web Firsts 100

blurb: First flights, first steps and history-making firsts

questions.q: In 1903, the Wright brothers made their first powered airplane flights near which town?
questions.fact: The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet.
questions.src: ncpedia.org/airplane-first-flight: about 12 s and 120 ft, Kill Devil Hill four miles south of Kitty Hawk. Reworded to 'their first' so the Whitehead first-flight claim can't be raised

questions.q: In 1932, who became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic?
questions.fact: She took off from Newfoundland and landed in a pasture in Northern Ireland.
questions.src: faa.gov blog pilot-many-firsts-amelia-earhart: Harbour Grace to a pasture near Culmore, N. Ireland; first woman to fly the Atlantic solo. Markham's flight 1936

questions.q: In 2021, Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet. What kind of aircraft was it?
questions.fact: It carried a tiny swatch of fabric from the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer.
questions.src: phys.org 2021-03 wright-brothers-1st-airplane-nasa: postage-size muslin from the Flyer's wing on Ingenuity; first flight April 19, 2021

questions.q: Bessie Coleman, the first African American woman to earn a pilot's license, trained in which country?
questions.fact: US flight schools would not admit her, so she studied French in Chicago and earned her license in 1921.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Coleman: US schools admitted neither women nor Black people; Berlitz French class in Chicago; FAI license in France June 15, 1921

questions.q: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.fact: She won in physics in 1903, then won again in chemistry in 1911.
questions.src: nobelprize.org (textbook): Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911

questions.q: Edmund Hillary, who first summited Everest with Tenzing Norgay in 1953, came from which country?
questions.fact: News of their May 29 climb reached London on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_British_Mount_Everest_expedition: summit May 29, news released in London the morning of June 2, coronation day; Hillary a New Zealander

questions.q: Whose team was the first to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
questions.fact: Amundsen's Norwegian team beat Robert Falcon Scott's British party by about five weeks.
questions.src: historyhit.com scott-vs-amundsen: Amundsen 14 Dec 1911, Scott 17 Jan 1912 (34 days, about five weeks)

questions.q: In 1665, Robert Hooke first used the word 'cell' in biology after viewing what under a microscope?
questions.fact: In his book Micrographia, he described the cork as full of tiny pores, much like a honeycomb.
questions.src: b-s-h.org.uk 'Much like a honey comb': Hooke saw cork full of tiny pores he called cells, Micrographia 1665. Old fact's monks'-rooms story is disputed; 'coined the word' fixed (the word existed)

questions.q: In 1947, Jackie Robinson broke baseball's modern color barrier with which team?
questions.fact: That season he won MLB's first Rookie of the Year award, which was later renamed in his honor.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB_Rookie_of_the_Year_Award: Robinson won the first (1947); renamed Jackie Robinson Award 1987. Old 'No. 42' fact duplicated A7 sports-legends Diamond Greats 100

questions.q: In 1954, who became the first person to run a mile in under four minutes?
questions.fact: He was a medical student and ran 3:59.4 on a track in Oxford, England.
questions.src: history.com this-day first-four-minute-mile: 25-year-old medical student, 3:59.4, Iffley Road track, Oxford

questions.q: Which country hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup, in 1930?
questions.fact: Uruguay beat neighbor Argentina 4-2 in the final in Montevideo.
questions.src: FIFA history (textbook): Uruguay 4-2 Argentina, Montevideo, 1930

questions.q: At the 1999 X Games, Tony Hawk became the first skater to land which trick?
questions.fact: A 900 is two and a half full spins in midair.
questions.src: guinnessworldrecords.com first-900-on-a-skateboard: Tony Hawk, 27 June 1999, X Games, San Francisco

blurb: Numbers, measures and math curiosities, big and small

questions.q: Pi Day is celebrated on which date, matching the first digits of pi?
questions.fact: The first big Pi Day party was held in 1988 at San Francisco's Exploratorium. It's also Einstein's birthday.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi_Day: earliest large-scale celebration 1988, Larry Shaw, Exploratorium; March 14 is Einstein's birthday

questions.q: In the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, which number comes next?
questions.fact: Fibonacci's 1202 book Liber Abaci helped bring Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe.
questions.src: Math (5 + 8 = 13); textbook history of Liber Abaci (1202)

questions.q: In Roman numerals, what number is written as XL?
questions.fact: A smaller numeral placed before a larger one is subtracted, so XL means 50 minus 10.
questions.src: Math / textbook Roman numerals (X=10, L=50, C=100; XL=40, LX=60, XC=90, CX=110). Replaces googol Q, which duplicated A2 log-on Garage Startups 200

questions.q: A number equal to the sum of its smaller divisors, like 6 (1+2+3), is called what?
questions.fact: The next perfect number is 28, since 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28.
questions.src: Math (definition of perfect number)

questions.q: How many feet are in a mile?
questions.fact: An English law of 1593, under Queen Elizabeth I, fixed the mile at 5,280 feet.
questions.src: encyclopedia.com Mile, Nautical and Statute: fixed at 5,280 ft (8 furlongs) by a 1593 act under Elizabeth I. 1,760 = yards in a mile

questions.q: A speed of one knot means traveling one what per hour?
questions.fact: Sailors once timed a knotted rope paying out behind the ship to gauge their speed.
questions.src: Textbook (knot = 1 nautical mile per hour; chip log with knotted line)

questions.q: A 'hand,' used to measure a horse's height, equals how many inches?
questions.fact: Horses are measured from the ground to the withers, the ridge between the shoulder blades.
questions.src: Textbook (1 hand = 4 inches)

questions.q: The metric system was first adopted in the 1790s by which country?
questions.fact: The meter was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
questions.src: Textbook (French Revolution metric system; original meter definition)

questions.q: How many keys are on a standard modern piano?
questions.fact: That's 52 white keys and 36 black keys.
questions.src: Textbook

questions.q: In the US, how many zeros are in one billion?
questions.fact: In older British usage, a billion meant a million million, with 12 zeros.
questions.src: Textbook (short scale vs long scale)

questions.q: How many items are in a 'gross'?
questions.fact: A gross is a dozen dozens, and a 'great gross' is 12 gross, or 1,728.

questions.q: In binary code, what number does 1010 represent?
questions.fact: Each binary place is worth double the one to its right: 8, 4, 2 and 1.

blurb: Calendars, clocks, time zones and how the months got their names

questions.q: Which month is named after Julius Caesar?
questions.fact: Caesar was born in that month, and the Romans renamed it in his honor in 44 BC.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintilis: renamed Iulius in 44 BC, Caesar's birth month

questions.q: January is named for Janus, the Roman god of what?
questions.fact: Janus had two faces, one looking back at the past and one looking ahead to the future.
questions.src: Textbook Roman mythology

questions.q: October comes from the Latin word for 'eight.' Why isn't it the 8th month?
options: The year once began in March
questions.fact: September, November and December likewise come from the Latin for seven, nine and ten.
questions.src: Textbook (early Roman calendar began in March)

questions.q: Before it was renamed for Emperor Augustus, what was the month of August called?
questions.fact: Quintilis, meaning 'fifth,' was the old name of July, the month just before it.
questions.src: Textbook (Sextilis renamed Augustus, 8 BC; Quintilis = July)

questions.q: Which ancient timekeeper tells the hour by the shadow it casts?
questions.fact: The part of a sundial that casts the shadow is called the gnomon.
questions.src: Textbook

questions.q: Greenwich, home of Greenwich Mean Time, is part of which city?
questions.fact: An 1884 conference in Washington, D.C., chose Greenwich as the Prime Meridian, 0 degrees longitude.
questions.src: Textbook (International Meridian Conference, 1884)

questions.q: In which year did US and Canadian railroads adopt standard time zones?
questions.fact: Before then, towns set clocks by the local sun, so neighboring cities often differed by minutes.
questions.src: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_time_in_the_United_States: US and Canadian railroads adopted standard time Nov 18, 1883; Standard Time Act 1918

questions.q: In 1967, scientists defined the second using the vibrations of which element's atoms?
questions.fact: That definition set one second at 9,192,631,770 cycles of radiation from a cesium-133 atom.
questions.src: BIPM SI definition of the second (13th CGPM, 1967). Fact reworded so it stays true if the second is ever redefined

questions.q: How many days are in a leap year?
questions.fact: The extra day keeps the calendar in step with Earth's trip around the sun, about 365.24 days.
questions.src: Textbook

questions.q: Which day of the week is named after the Norse god Thor?
questions.fact: Wednesday honors Woden, or Odin, who was Thor's father in Norse myth.
questions.src: Textbook etymology

questions.q: When Britain and its colonies switched calendars in 1752, how many days were skipped?
questions.fact: That's why George Washington's birthday moved from February 11 to February 22.
questions.src: mountvernon.org celebrating Washington's birthday: Feb 11 old style became Feb 22 after the 1752 change (11 days). 10 days = 1582 switch

questions.q: Under Gregorian calendar rules, which of these century years was a leap year?
questions.fact: Century years must divide evenly by 400 to be leap years, so the next one is 2400.
questions.src: Math / Gregorian rule
